senses.gloss:
māṁsabhakṣaṇa
(‘eating of flesh’)
------------------------------------------
Māṁsabhakṣaṇa, eating of flesh or meat, has been a subject hotly discussed in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. During the early Vedic period, as also during the period of the उपनिषद्स्, ड़्लेस्ह्-एअतिन्ग्, including beef, seems to have been quite common. It was a part of the मधुपर्क usually offered to an honoured guest (vide आश्वलायन Gṛhyasūtra 1.24.25). Apart from the क्षत्त्रिय kings even the sages like Yājña-valkya have been mentioned as consuming meat (vide Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 3.1.2.21). Animals immolated in sacrifices—like horse, ox, goat and ram—were cooked and eaten (vide ऐतरेय Brāhmaṇa 6.8).
However, as the आर्यन्स् moved towards the Indo-Gangetic plains and cultivation of ड़ोओद्-crops picked up in momen-tum, eating of the flesh of animals gradually reduced and was even looked down upon. The growth of जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् also delivered a powerful blow to this practice.
Development of the doctrine of अहिṁसा, gradual replacement of the Vedic sacrificial religion by the paurāṇic modes of worship and the भागवत-cult, contri-buted to the disappearance or minimisation of the practice of eating meat.
Protection of the cow, the roots of which are found even in the Ṛgveda (1.164.27; 4.1.6; 8.69.21), became an article of faith with the whole Hindu society.
Now, even those who have been meat eaters for ages, have either given it up or take it only occasionally and not daily.

māṁsāhāra
(‘meat as ड़ोओद्’)
------------------------------------------
The ड़ोओद् that a human being consumes may be sasyāhāra (vegetarian ड़ोओद्) or माṁसाहार (non-vegetarian ड़ोओद्, flesh or meat).
Though माṁसाहार was quite common in the earlier ages, it was gradually superseded by sasyāhāra because the latter came to be considered as more sāttvik and hence more conducive to spiritual pursuits.
The spread of Vedāntic ideas as also जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म् contributed not a little to this trend.
See also MĀṀSABHAKṢAṆA.
